title: Why Obesity Care Is a Journey, Not a Finish Line
summary: When Jacqueline’s family began to express concerns about her health, it landed as a wake-up call.
body_markdown:
When Jacqueline's family began to express concerns about her health, it landed as a wake-up call. Over time, her weight changed and she became concerned about her risk of heart disease and diabetes, which ran in her family.


*This article first appeared in Mediaplanet's November 2026 Future of Obesity Care campaign, which was distributed in USA Today, and is reposted with permission.*


“I knew I needed to make a change,” Jacqueline said. After setting her mind to managing her weight, Jacqueline made a number of lifestyle changes. “I tried workout plans, eating plans, I even hired a dietitian before my wedding,” she said.


Like many people living with obesity, she found that early progress did not always translate into lasting results. “Each helped at first, but I always went back to 'normal' and gained again,” she said.


The frustration of “yo-yo diet after yo-yo diet not sticking,” in Jacqueline's words, led her to talk to her care team about GLP-1 treatment.


Upon treatment, Jacqueline began to see progress in managing her obesity.


After losing weight with a combination of treatment, diet and exercise, Jacqueline wanted to see whether she could maintain that progress without medication. Within a month, she noticed her original struggles returning. By three months, she had regained the weight she had lost and decided to restart GLP-1 treatment.


As she explored her options, Jacqueline's understanding of obesity evolved. Her experience helped her recognize obesity as a chronic disease shaped by a complex mix of biology, genetics, social determinants, and appetite regulation.


“My doctor really helped me refocus what I thought about obesity,” Jacqueline said. “He says I have a dysregulated appetite; that my brain wants to keep going and ignores or doesn't receive satiety cues.


Obesity isn't a lack of willpower; it's my brain fighting against me.”


That shift helped Jacqueline begin letting go of the stigma surrounding treatment. With support from her care team and her family, she felt better equipped to manage her obesity as a chronic disease. It also gave her the confidence to speak more openly about her experience.


“I want to scream from the rooftops about how this medicine helped me,” she said. “I want to reframe the narrative and share what a helpful tool this can be.”


For Jacqueline, success isn't solely defined by a number on the scale. On a recent vacation with her husband, she was able to walk more than she felt she had in the past. “I wouldn't have been able to do that before, and I would've felt embarrassed,” she said. “Success to me is being able to feel more confident, even if others called the method 'cheating' at first,” Jacqueline said. “Spoiler: They don't anymore.”


Jacqueline knows that no two experiences with obesity are the same, but her own journey reinforced that obesity is a chronic disease requiring ongoing management.


“I'm living the life I want with the knowledge and support to keep moving forward,” she said.


While success may look different for everyone, she hopes more open conversations can help people seek the information, support, and individualized care they need to manage a chronic disease over the long term.
